summary: Suggests defining a single access protocol, using one reserved socket, as the front door to the network's standard services. Commands such as USER, PASS, ACCT, MAIL, FTP and HELP would select the service wanted, and the proposed mail protocol could be the first to use it.

eli5.summary: Instead of a separate door for each service, why not one front door where you say who you are and which room you want? This note proposes that.

subtitle: One login for all network services instead of a separate entry point for each.

tldr.problem: Each network protocol (mail, FTP, remote job submission) had its own entry point and login mechanism, forcing users to learn multiple access patterns.
tldr.mechanism: Define a single unified access protocol with a reserved socket where users log in once with USER, PASS, and ACCT commands, then select their service (MAIL, FTP, RJS, DRS, etc.) from a menu.
tldr.outcome: The proposal is simple enough to specify and implement, potentially allowing mail to be the first protocol adopted under this unified model.

today: This proposal predates unified protocols like Telnet-based access and modern authentication systems. The concept of a single entry point for multiple services eventually appeared in modern systems, though not in the form described here.

sections.title: Too Many Front Doors
sections.content:
Network protocols in 1973 each required separate connection and login: FTP had one entry point, mail had another, remote job submission (RJS) had its own. Users had to authenticate separately at each protocol, learning different command sets and behavior.

The author asks: why not specify a single access protocol with one reserved socket before the mail protocol becomes official? This unified entry point could be simple and flexible enough that protocols could be moved to it at the convenience of their implementors.
sections.eli5: You have to log in to mail, then log in to file transfer, then log in to job submission. Why not one login that lets you pick what you want?

sections.title: The Unified Protocol Structure
sections.content:
The proposal outlines commands for this unified access layer: USER, PASS, and ACCT would handle authentication. MAIL, FTP, RJS, and DRS would select the service. A HELP command and BYE to disconnect round out the set.

The commands would nest following a model of command and reply spaces (referenced from Jim White's earlier work). This approach does not address what resources are free to use or how protocols interrelate, but it does not worsen those problems—it just structures them differently.
sections.eli5: Say USER and your name, PASS and your password, then pick MAIL or FTP or another service from a menu. The nested commands let each service have its own sub-commands underneath.

sections.title: Benefits of Unified Access
sections.content:
A single reserved socket for all standard protocols would simplify user experience. Instead of learning separate login procedures for mail, FTP, and other services, users would authenticate once and then select their service. This is simple enough to specify and implement before the proposed mail protocol becomes official.

The proposal suggests that the new mail protocol could be the first to use this unified access framework, with other protocols moved over as their specifications stabilize and implementors are ready.
sections.eli5: One login for mail, one for FTP, one for remote jobs—it is confusing. One login that lets you pick which service keeps things simple.
